lesson.title: The Slowest Climb: Why Logarithms Barely Grow at All
lesson.summary: Logarithmic functions increase without bound, but so slowly that they lose a growth race to every positive power of x, a direct mirror image of how exponential functions grow explosively fast.
lesson.body:
A logarithmic function such as f(x) = log_b(x) does increase forever as x increases, since larger inputs always produce larger outputs, but it does so at a pace that keeps decelerating. This makes logarithmic growth the slowest broad category encountered when comparing growth rates: a logarithm eventually loses a growth race not just to exponential functions, but to any positive power of x, even a small power like the square root.

Compare f(x) = ln(x) and g(x) = sqrt(x) = x^(1/2). At x=100, f(100) = ln(100), approximately 4.605, while g(100) = 10, already well ahead. At x=10,000, f(10,000) = ln(10,000), approximately 9.210, while g(10,000) = 100. At x=1,000,000, f(1,000,000) = ln(1,000,000), approximately 13.816, while g(1,000,000) = 1,000. Notice the pattern: multiplying x by 100 only adds about 4.605 to the logarithm's value each time, since ln(100x) = ln(100) + ln(x), but it multiplies the square root's value by 10 each time. The gap between them widens without limit, confirming lim x to infinity of ln(x)/sqrt(x) = 0, even though the square root is one of the slowest-growing polynomial powers available.

The mechanism behind this sluggish growth is the defining algebraic property of logarithms: log_b(xy) = log_b(x) + log_b(y). This turns multiplication of the input into addition of the output, so multiplying x by a fixed factor, say 10, only ever adds a fixed constant to the output, log_b(10), no matter how large x already was. A function that needs its input multiplied, not just added to, in order to gain a fixed amount of output is fundamentally the slowest kind of unbounded growth, since exponential growth in the input would be required just to produce steady, linear growth in the output.

Different logarithmic bases do not change this slow-growth conclusion, only the constant of proportionality. Since log_b(x) = ln(x)/ln(b) for any valid base b, two logarithms with different bases are always constant multiples of one another: for instance log_2(x) = ln(x)/ln(2), so log_2(x)/ln(x) = 1/ln(2), a fixed constant, approximately 1.443, for every x. This means comparing growth rates of log_2(x) against ln(x) gives a finite nonzero limit rather than 0 or infinity, so all logarithms, regardless of base, belong to the same slow-growing family and are considered to grow at the same rate as one another.

This is the exact mirror image of exponential growth rate, where a fixed additive step in x produces a fixed multiplicative change in output. Logarithmic functions are the inverse of exponential functions, so it makes sense that their growth behaviors sit at opposite extremes: one is the fastest common category of growth, the other is the slowest, and every polynomial power of x sits strictly between them on the growth rate hierarchy, no matter how small or how large the polynomial's exponent is.

Practically, this means that in any comparison lim x to infinity of log_b(x)/x^p for any positive number p, however small, the limit is always 0. Logarithmic terms can therefore be treated as negligible next to any positive power of x when determining the end behavior of a more complicated expression that mixes logarithmic and polynomial pieces.
